title: Coding Basics · Episode 3
chapters: Y2K: the disaster that didn't happen

units.t: Coding Basics. Episode three.
In this episode: How websites work, Bugs and debugging and Y2K: the disaster that didn't happen.
Part one. How websites work.
Type a web address and a page appears in under a second.
Behind that blink is a relay race across the planet.
Browsers and servers.
Every website visit is a conversation between two computers.
Your browser, such as Safari, Chrome, Firefox or Edge, is the client: it asks for things.
A server is a computer, usually in a data centre, that stores a website's files and sends them out when asked.
Servers are simply computers built to run all day and answer many requests at once.
Big sites run on thousands of them around the world.
The first web server was a NeXT computer in Tim Berners-Lee's office at CERN, with a handwritten label warning colleagues not to switch it off.
The first website, info.
cern.
ch, went live in 1991.
In 1993 the Mosaic browser displayed pictures alongside text, and public interest exploded.
Reading a web address.
Computers find each other with numeric IP addresses, but people use domain names, which have a structure.
Read abc.
net.
au from right to left: .
au is Australia's country-code ending.
net.
au is a category within it, and abc is the name its owner registered.
Australian names are overseen by auDA, a not-for-profit body.
Since 2022, anyone with an Australian connection can register directly under .
au, such as example.
au.
Domain names are rented, not owned outright.
You pay a registrar for one to five years at a time, and if you forget to renew, someone else can grab the name.
HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
Web pages use three main languages.
HTML, HyperText Markup Language, describes what is on the page: this is a heading, this is a paragraph, here is an image, this text links to another page.
It is the frame and rooms of a house.
Tags wrap around content to mark where each element begins and ends.
Links, the feature that makes the web a web, are part of HTML.
CSS, Cascading Style Sheets, is the paint and furniture: colours, fonts, spacing and layout, rearranged to fit a phone or a big monitor.
JavaScript is the wiring and plumbing.
When a menu slides open or a form warns you've missed your postcode, JavaScript is at work.
Keeping the three separate makes sites easier to build and redesign.
From address to page.
When you type an address and press enter, your browser first uses DNS to find the server's numeric address.
It opens a connection and, for secure sites, agrees on encryption, shown by the padlock.
It sends a request using rules called HTTP.
The server responds with HTML.
The browser discovers it also needs images, fonts, CSS and JavaScript, requests those, and assembles the page, often within a second.
Developers split the work in two.
The front end runs in your browser: layout, buttons and animations.
The back end runs on servers, handling things you don't see, like checking your password or storing your order.
At checkout, the front end collects your details while the back end processes payment, updates stock and triggers a confirmation email.
Browsing smarter.
HTTPS and the padlock mean your connection to a site is encrypted, so others on the network can't read it.
They do not mean the site is honest; scam sites use HTTPS too.
Always check the domain name carefully, since scammers register look-alike addresses, such as an extra letter or a different ending.
Cookies are small files that sites store in your browser to remember logins and preferences, and sometimes to track you across sites.
Your browser settings let you view and clear them.
Knowing how the web works is one of the simplest ways to stay safe on it.
The key idea: A browser on your device requests files from a server, a computer that stores and sends out the website.
Part two. Bugs and debugging.
A moth in a relay, a rocket lost in under a minute, and a rubber duck on a desk: the surprising story of how software goes wrong and gets fixed.
What a bug is.
A bug is an error that makes a program crash, freeze, show the wrong number or open a security hole.
Most bugs are not the computer's fault: it did exactly what it was told, and the instructions were wrong or incomplete.
Large programs are enormously complex and people make mistakes, so bugs are unavoidable.
Debugging, tracking them down, is one of the most important skills in programming.
On 9 September 1947, operators of the Harvard Mark II traced a fault to a moth trapped in a relay and taped it into the logbook: 'First actual case of bug being found.'
The joke worked because engineers already called faults 'bugs'; Thomas Edison used the word in the 1870s.
The page is held by the Smithsonian.
Kinds of bugs.
Syntax errors are like spelling or grammar mistakes, such as a missing bracket, and the computer usually refuses to run until they're fixed.
Logic errors are sneakier: the program runs happily but gives the wrong answer, like a discount that subtracts 10 dollars instead of 10 percent.
Then there are edge cases, unusual situations the programmer didn't think of.
What if a surname has an apostrophe, a customer orders zero items, or a date falls on 29 February?
Many real-world bugs live at these edges.
Debugging systematically.
Effective debugging is closer to detective work than guesswork.
First, reproduce the bug reliably: exactly what actions make it happen?
Next, narrow down where it occurs by checking the program's values at different points.
A handy trick is halving: if the problem is somewhere in 1,000 lines, check the middle, then keep halving.
Then form a theory about the cause, change one thing, and test again.
Changing many things at once may make the bug vanish without revealing why, and it may come back.
The 1999 book The Pragmatic Programmer tells of a programmer who explained code line by line to a rubber duck.
Explaining forces you to state what each step actually does, rather than what you assume, and the gap is often where the bug hides.
Costly bugs.
On 4 June 1996, the first Ariane 5 rocket veered off course and was destroyed about 40 seconds after launch, with four scientific satellites aboard.
Guidance code reused from Ariane 4 tried to squeeze a large number, related to horizontal speed, into a space too small.
Ariane 5 was faster, so it overflowed and the system shut down.
The backup ran identical software and failed the same way.
The loss is often estimated at several hundred million US dollars.
For decades, many programs stored years as two digits to save memory, so 1999 was just 99.
The worry was that 00 would be read as 1900.
Governments and businesses, including in Australia, spent enormous sums fixing code.
Problems were mostly minor.
Some argue the threat was exaggerated, but many experts credit the repair effort.
Lessons for everyone.
Bugs affect everyone, not just programmers.
Software updates often fix bugs, including security flaws, so installing them promptly is one of the simplest ways to stay safe.
When reporting a problem to a company or IT help desk, describe it like a debugger would: what you did, what you expected, what actually happened, and whether you can make it happen again.
The same mindset works for a car that won't start or a recipe that failed.
Reproduce the problem, change one thing at a time, and explain it out loud.
Sometimes the duck knows best.
The key idea: A bug is a mistake in software that makes it behave in ways its creators didn't intend.
Part three. Y2K: the disaster that didn't happen.
As 1999 drew to a close, the world braced for computers to think it was 1900.
Midnight came and almost nothing broke.
Was it all hype, or one of history's great quiet successes?
Saving two digits.
In the 1960s and 1970s computer memory and storage were astonishingly expensive, and a standard punch card had only 80 columns.
Programmers saved space by writing years as two digits: 68 instead of 1968.
Few expected the programs to last decades, yet many did.
Banking, payroll, airline and government systems were built in layers on old code, often in COBOL, and rarely replaced.
By the 1990s vast amounts of software assumed every year began with 19.
When the calendar ticked over to 2000, the year 00 might be read as 1900.
The problem became known as Y2K, short for Year 2000.
Arithmetic, not explosions.
The fear was never that computers would explode.
It was arithmetic.
If a system works out age by subtracting birth year from the current year, 00 minus 65 gives minus 65.
Interest, card expiry dates, warranties and record deletion all rely on comparing dates, and a sorted list might put 2000 before 1999.
Some programs also failed to treat 2000 as a leap year, because century years are leap years only if divisible by 400.
Tiny processors sit in lifts, power stations and medical devices, and nobody had a full list of which tracked dates.
Most did not, but organisations could not know without testing.
The worry was many failures at once, in connected systems.
The great repair job.
Through the late 1990s, programmers combed through old code line by line, and retired COBOL experts were in demand again.
Common fixes were expanding years to four digits, or 'windowing', where a program treats two-digit years below a cut-off, say 50, as 20xx and the rest as 19xx.
Worldwide cost estimates vary widely, often falling between 300 and 600 billion US dollars.
Australia, like many countries, ran national awareness and readiness programs, and governments set up command centres to monitor the changeover.
Some critics said much of the money went to overcautious consultants.
Others noted that the work also cleaned up and documented ageing systems that needed attention anyway.
Midnight arrives.
Australia and the Pacific reached midnight hours before Europe and North America, so the world watched them for early signs of trouble.
None came on a large scale.
There were glitches.
Some websites showed the year as 19100, because programs added 1900 to the year, and a few ticketing and payment machines misbehaved.
In Japan some monitoring equipment at nuclear plants reported errors, without any danger to safety.
A US military satellite intelligence system had several hours of problems.
Most faults were fixed quickly and passed almost unnoticed.
Within days, some newspapers that had warned of chaos were asking whether it had all been a beat-up.
The preparedness paradox.
Y2K is a classic case of the preparedness paradox: fix a problem before it bites, and the lack of disaster can make the warning look silly.
Experts still debate how bad things would have been.
Some countries that spent little also had few problems, partly because they relied less on old systems.
Yet many who did the work insist they found serious faults that would have caused real damage.
Date bugs have not gone away.
Many systems count seconds since 1 January 1970, and where that count is stored as a 32-bit number it will overflow on 19 January 2038.
Much software has been updated, but the next deadline is ticking.
The key idea: Programmers wrote years as two digits to save scarce memory, leaving old software that might read 2000 as 1900.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is a web server?
Answer. A computer that stores and sends out a website.
Question two. Why are most software bugs not the computer's fault?
Answer. It did exactly what it was told, by flawed instructions.
Question three. Why did programmers write years with only two digits?
Answer. Memory and storage were expensive, so they saved space.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
